_comment: Numbers the page renders. Upload a new copy of this file and the page
updates — no HTML change, no redeploy of anything else.
`decode` is a best recorded rate on that machine, or null for 'not
measured'. Null renders as 'not measured' rather than a blank or a zero,
because a missing measurement and a slow one are different claims.
`modes` is how the model runs there: gpu = fully resident, ssd = experts
stream from disk, hyb = split CPU/GPU. Several modes means the app can
use any of them; an empty list renders 'does not fit'.
`os` and `backend` drive the two tab rows. os is mac|linux; backend is
metal|cuda|rocm|cann. Choosing an OS disables the backends that cannot run
on it, and the machine, post and download lists all filter to the pair.
A backend with no machine yet (cann) still renders a tab, disabled, because
'no measurement yet' and 'not supported' are different claims.
_provenance: The M4 mini and DGX Spark rows were measured directly on those machines in August 2026 and carry the method in their notes. On 12 August 2026 three M1 Ultra rows were re-measured the same way and now carry medians with spreads: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Laguna-S-2.1 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Where a re-measurement moved a number it is recorded here rather than silently overwritten: Laguna-S-2.1 30.8 -> 33.4 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash 27.5 -> 28.0 (both faster than published), Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 73.7 -> 72.3. The M1 Ultra DeepSeek-V4-Flash size was corrected from 97.6 GB to 87 GB: the old figure matched no file on the machine and disagreed with the same model's own M2 Max and DGX Spark rows. A fourth attempt, M2 Max Qwen3-4B, was WITHDRAWN rather than published: two runs of the identical script disagreed by 1.7x, so that row is now null. TWO LIMITS THIS EXERCISE EXPOSED, which apply to every row on this page. First, decode is not a single rate: measured on M2 Max, the 1->129 token slope and the 129->513 slope differ by 15%, because attention costs more as the context grows -- so any figure here depends on the token count it was taken at, which is 129. Second, these machines are shared, and a busy machine can halve the number; spreads are quoted so a reader can see when that happened. The remaining M1 Ultra and M2 Max rows are still carried over verbatim from the first version of this page and have NOT been re-verified. Prices are approximate street or list prices in August 2026, recorded so a rate can be read against what the machine costs -- they move, and they are not quotes. Muse Glimmer 30B was ADDED to the M1 Ultra and M2 Max boxes after the 12 August exercise and does not share its method: both figures are llama.cpp's llama-bench tg128 (build b10360, r=3, 12 August 2026), an instrument reporting a mean over repetitions rather than the median-of-paired-estimates used elsewhere here, so the two rows are comparable with each other but not strictly with their neighbours, and the notes say so. Where two runs exist the LOWER is published: M2 Max decode 6.42 and 6.25 -> 6.3, prefill 82.65 and 76.75 -> 78. Two figures also exist for the M1 Ultra and both are kept rather than one being chosen silently: tg128 23.20 and tg64 ~28.9. tg128 is published because the rest of the column is quoted at 129 generated tokens; the tg64 figure is not wrong, it is a shorter generation, which this page already records as producing a higher rate. The tg64 run is documented as having a ds4 Q4_K kernel substitution active and the tg128 runs do not say, which is why these rows decline to name an engine's kernels the way their neighbours do. These are also the only two rows on this page measured on TWO machines by one instrument, and the 0.28x ratio between them against a 0.605 tier prediction is the reason no rate here is scaled from another machine's. In late August 2026 a fifth box was added: an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 (Strix Halo), running the same DeepSeek-V4-Flash file as the DGX Spark row through the ROCm reference engine, at 15.0 tok/s decode. It is published at the machine's default power governor rather than at its best observed setting, because the default is what a buyer gets; forcing the GPU to `high` is worth +0.8% on decode and +6.7% on prefill, and up to +26% when the CPU is also busy, but it costs a co-running CPU job about 40% and was still showing 104C peaks after 25 minutes of soak, so it is not a free setting and is not what the row reports. The machine's NPU is excluded from the figure for the plainer reason that it was measured and is worth +0.4%. The Ryzen row's price is what was actually paid for the machine (£3,099, Bosgame M5, August 2026) rather than a list price, which is why it is the only row in a currency other than dollars; it has not been converted, because a made-up exchange rate is not better provenance than none. On 29 August 2026 two rows were added to the M1 Ultra table, each measured on that machine: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next at 30.8 tok/s and GLM-5.3-Flash at 24.1 tok/s. The GLM-5.2 row (3.5 tok/s, SSD-streamed) was removed rather than re-measured, because the model is no longer offered; its number was not superseded by a new measurement of the same model and is not claimed to be wrong. An Atlas A2 row (8x 910B2, 512 GB) was added in late August 2026 with a NULL decode rate: the ds4-rs-ascend binary is built and verified to install on that hardware, but DeepSeek-V4-Flash has not been run on it, and 'packaged' is not 'measured'. Its price is left blank: A2 systems have no citable list figure, and every other price here names a source, so an estimate was dropped rather than published as though it were sourced. FULL METHOD for the M1 Ultra rows, moved out of the rendered note on 2026-08-29 because that note had grown to 3,074 characters against 520 for the shortest box: Three of these six rows were re-measured on this machine on 12 August 2026; the figure is the median of paired estimates, not a best-ever run. Decode is isolated as the difference between a 129-token and a 1-token completion so prefill is excluded, and repetitions alternate A/B/B/A so drift lands on both arms. Each model runs on the engine the app picks for it, and they are not the same engine: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on llama.cpp with the ds4 kernels — 72.3, ten estimates spanning 67.5–78.0; Laguna-S-2.1 on the ds4 reference engine — 33.4, eight estimates spanning 33.1–34.3; DeepSeek-V4-Flash on our own Rust/Metal engine — 28.0, eight estimates spanning 27.8–28.2. The machine was shared with other work throughout, which is why the Qwen3.6 spread is the wide one; the DeepSeek figure independently reproduces a 27.9–28.2 anchor measured by a different harness. The last two rows are out-of-core rates and are still carried over unverified: GLM-5.2 is not present on this machine at all, and Kimi-K3 is present but its streaming mode is the untested claim — one attempt at an out-of-core model of that class drove the machine into 42 GB of swap and was stopped. Muse Glimmer 30B is measured by a different instrument and is marked so rather than blended in: llama.cpp's own llama-bench, build b10360, on 12 August 2026 — tg128 23.20 ± 0.19 over three repetitions, with a pp512 prefill of 247.55 ± 0.87. That is a mean over repetitions, not the median of paired estimates the rows above use. It is quoted at 128 generated tokens because that is nearest the 129 the rest of the column uses; the same model on this machine was separately recorded at ~28.9 tok/s on tg64, and that gap between 64 and 128 tokens is the context effect described below, not a contradiction. llama.cpp is the only engine that can load this architecture — our own engine has no path for it — but which of the two Q4_K matvec paths that run used is not recorded, so unlike the rows above this one names no kernels. Two rows were added on 29 August 2026 and both were measured on this machine. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next — 30.8, the median of three llama-bench tg128 repetitions (30.78 ± 0.03), running on llama.cpp; its prefill is 560.7 tok/s at pp512. GLM-5.3-Flash — 24.1, on the ds4 reference engine, fully GPU-resident at 32K context; the same model measures 17.6 at a 9,600-token prompt, so the headline is a short-context figure like the others on this table and long sessions are slower. GLM-5.2 has been removed from this row. It never fit in memory on a 128 GB machine — 216.7 GB, streamed from SSD — and GLM-5.3-Flash now runs resident on the same hardware at roughly seven times the rate, so the older model is no longer offered. The Atlas A2 note was removed from the rendered page on 2026-08-29 as telling the reader nothing the table already showed (decode is null, which renders as 'not measured'; price is null, which renders as nothing). Its content, for the record: A Huawei Atlas A2 server: eight Ascend 910B2 cards, 64 GB HBM each, 512 GB in total, confirmed from npu-smi on the box (8 chips, 65536 MB per chip, all reporting healthy). DeepSeek-V4-Flash has not been measured here. The ds4-rs-ascend controller is built and published for this hardware and installs on it, but no decode rate has been taken, so none is quoted — the row says 'not measured' rather than borrowing a number from another machine. An 87 GB model fits resident many times over in 512 GB, which is why the residency column reads GPU; that is an arithmetic claim about capacity, not a measurement of speed. No price is shown. A2 systems sell through configuration-dependent channels with no list figure to cite, and every other price on this page names a source — a list price, or an amount actually paid. An unsourced estimate would be the odd one out, so the field is left empty until there is something to point at. FULL METHOD for the Ryzen AI Max+ 395 and M2 Max rows, moved out of the rendered notes on 2026-08-29 for the same reason as the M1 Ultra's: the page carried more method than a reader of a comparison table needs. AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395: The same DeepSeek-V4-Flash file as the DGX Spark row, 86.7 GB on disk, on a Bosgame M5 mini-PC (AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 “Strix Halo”, Radeon 8060S, 128 GB LPDDR5X, 2 TB SSD) through the reference ROCm engine, so the model and the quantisation are comparable to the Mac rows even though the engine is not. Measured August 2026 at a 2048-token context; eight baseline repetitions spanned 0.03 tok/s (15.00–15.03) and the GPU clock was sampled throughout (1707 MHz mean). The weights sit in unified memory rather than streaming, which is why an 87 GB model reports a resident rate on a 128 GB box. The price is what was paid, not a list figure, and it is worth reading beside the DGX Spark row rather than instead of it: this machine is the cheaper of the two and the slower of the two on this model. Two things specific to it are worth stating rather than hiding. The rate depends on the GPU power governor: this figure is the out-of-the-box auto setting, and forcing high moves decode to 15.1 and prefill by 6.7% — a setting, not a property of the silicon. And its XDNA2 NPU, which no other box here has, was measured co-executing the output projection: it is worth +0.4%, so it is not used for this number. The 126 TOPS on the box is the platform total across NPU, GPU and CPU; the NPU's own share of it is 50. M2 Max: The same catalogue, scored for 64 GB. Qwen3-4B was measured twice here on 12 August 2026 and the two runs disagreed by 1.7× — 43.4 tok/s and then 74.9 tok/s from the identical script, model and engine. The first run was taken minutes after a 2.3 GB file landed on the machine, so the machine's state rather than the model dominated it. The row is therefore withdrawn rather than published at either figure: a number that does not mean what it says is worse than an admitted gap. It will return when it can be measured on a quiescent machine. The other three rows are still carried over from the first version of this page and have not been re-verified — this machine currently has 27 GB of disk free, so the 22 GB Qwen3.6 and the 48 GB Laguna-S cannot be stored without freeing space, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash at 87 GB is out-of-core here, which is what the 2.9 would cost. Muse Glimmer 30B was measured on both this machine and the M1 Ultra, by the same llama-bench instrument and in the same window — tg128 6.42 ± 0.08, and 6.25 ± 0.25 on a re-run, published at the lower 6.3; prefill 82.65 and 76.75 on the two runs, so ~78. The point of measuring it twice is what it says about every unmeasured row on this page: this machine delivers 0.28× the Ultra's rate, where scaling by GPU tier would have predicted 0.605 and advertised ~14 tok/s to a Mac that gives ~6.3. A control model measured on both boxes in the same window ran 3.0× slower here too, so this is the machine and not something peculiar to Muse Glimmer. This is also the smallest M2 Max — 30 of a possible 38 GPU cores — so a fuller Max should beat it. On 30 August 2026 the two dense Qwen3 rows were added to the M1 Ultra by the same 129-vs-1-token differencing used on the M4 mini, so the two machines' dense rows are directly comparable: Qwen3-4B 130.2 tok/s and Qwen3-8B 87.6 tok/s (medians of 5). Both ran on llama.cpp with the ds4 kernels, which is the engine the app picks for dense Qwen; the same models on our own Metal engine reach only 26.9 tok/s, which is why the engine is named per row rather than assumed. On 30 August 2026 the two M4 mini rows were re-measured and corrected UPWARDS: Qwen3-4B 19.6 -> 36.2 and Qwen3-8B 12.0 -> 21.6 tok/s. The published figures were ~1.8x low because they had been taken on a slower engine than the one the app now picks for dense Qwen; the corrected numbers come from the same 129-vs-1-token differencing as before, and are confirmed by a second instrument on the same box (llama-bench tg128: 37.9 and 21.6). Separately, the M2 Max Qwen3-4B row withdrawn earlier for a 1.7x disagreement between identical runs is now EXPLAINED rather than merely withdrawn: that laptop runs with Low Power Mode enabled, which costs it exactly 1.73x (69.7 vs 40.3 tok/s on the same model and binary). The row stays null until it can be measured with Low Power Mode off, because a battery setting is not a property of the chip. Also on 30 August 2026 the M2 Max column was re-measured with Low Power Mode OFF, and three rows moved UP: Muse Glimmer 30B 6.3 -> 8.5, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 51.6 -> 62.3, and Qwen3-4B filled in at 81.1 (the row withdrawn earlier for a 1.7x disagreement between identical runs — the disagreement was this setting). That laptop had Low Power Mode enabled for AC as well as battery, which costs about 2.1x on a small dispatch-bound model and about 1.4x on a bandwidth-bound one, and it does NOT recover on cooldown, which is what distinguishes it from thermal throttling. These three are llama-bench tg128 medians taken in a window verified quiet; the 129-vs-1 differencing used elsewhere agrees with llama-bench within 5% on the two machines where both could be run, but could not be re-run here because the laptop went back into interactive use. A second lesson is folded into these numbers: benchmarking several models back-to-back penalises whichever runs later — the 35B read 53 following two other models and 62 sampled on its own — so each figure here comes from a single-model series. The two M2 Max rows left carried-over on 30 August 2026 were then measured too, with Low Power Mode off. DeepSeek-V4-Flash went 2.9 -> 7.2 tok/s (median of 8 across two independent runs, 6.63-7.49); at 86.7 GB it cannot be resident on a 64 GB machine, so this is SSD-streaming with a 39.9 GB expert cache, and it is the one rate on this page that is disk-bound rather than memory-bound. Laguna-S-2.1 re-measured at 25.8 against its published 26.4, so that row was already right and is now verified rather than carried over; it was taken on the tile-rs engine, which an earlier campaign measured at parity (1.01x) with the reference engine the app uses for that model. No row on this machine is now unverified. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash joined in 1.0.6: 2.9 tok/s decode and 70 t/s prefill on the M1 Ultra with the file on the internal SSD, measured 13 September 2026 on a 2048-token prompt. Only ~152 GiB of the 366 GB file is weights; the engram tables are read a row at a time from the file, which is why it runs at all on a 128 GB Mac and why the drive matters: the same file decodes at 0.54 tok/s from an external USB SSD. It does not fit a 64 GB Mac. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next MTP joined in 1.0.7 and is the first model on this page measured on two machines by the same instrument in the same window since Muse Glimmer. It is antirez's Q2 file, 147 GB on disk, on his reference engine, run with multi-token prediction as the app runs it. It is a DIFFERENT FILE AND A DIFFERENT ENGINE from the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next row above it, which is Unsloth's UD-Q2_K_XL on llama.cpp at 30.8; the older row is kept rather than overwritten because it was not re-measured, and the two are not a before-and-after. Only about 45 GiB of the 147 GB file has to be resident: the per-layer embedding table, 95.37 GiB of it, is read a row at a time and never held in memory, which is the same disk-versus-memory split as the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash row and the reason a 147 GB model reports a GPU-resident rate on a 128 GB Mac and fits a 64 GB one. M1 ULTRA 128 GB, 2026-09-19, greedy, reference engine main 8db1d1d: 43.7-43.9 tok/s on open prose with 71.7% of drafts accepted, and 47.0-51.2 on code with 96.7%; 36.1-38.0 with MTP off. The prose figure is published because it is the LOWER of the two, the same rule used elsewhere on this page. Prefill is 498-516 t/s across 2k-8k frontiers on 2048-token chunks, published at 510. M2 MAX 64 GB, 2026-09-21, same binary and the --prefill-chunk 1024 the model's own notes advise for 64 GB: 23.6-24.3 tok/s on prose at the same 71.7% acceptance, 27.9-28.0 on code, ds4-bench steady decode 22.6/20.8/20.6/20.0 at 2k/4k/6k/8k, prefill 259/234/229/227, and a resident plan of exactly 43.19 GiB at 8192 context — so IT FITS. A CLAIM OF 50-60 tok/s ON A 64 GB MAC IS WHAT PROMPTED THIS MEASUREMENT AND IT IS NOT REPRODUCED: the best figure on the real machine is 28 tok/s, on code, which is the easiest content for a draft head, and plain decode is 16-23. The M2 Max lands at roughly 60% of the Ultra's decode and 45% of its prefill, which tracks memory bandwidth, and draft acceptance matches the Ultra's exactly at 71.7% on prose, so the shortfall is the HARDWARE and not the speculation. One caveat specific to this laptop, in the same family as the Low Power Mode finding above: the plain arms fell about 28% between the first and last pass, 23.3 down to 16.8 on prose, while the MTP arms held steady — the signature of a laptop-class chip under sustained load — so a range is published rather than a single number, and where in a run a figure was taken matters. One earlier claim is CORRECTED rather than quietly dropped: a run on the Ultra with 64 GiB locked away via --simulate-used-memory had reported the same speed as the full machine, and was cited as evidence about 64 GB Macs. That simulation was right about RESIDENCY — 43.19 GiB on both, which the real machine confirmed to the decimal — and wrong about SPEED, because locking memory away leaves the Ultra's memory bandwidth intact. Only the fit half survived contact with a real 64 GB Mac. Finally, the engine that generates every kernel for this architecture in our own compiler is verified bit-identical to the reference engine and measures 4.8-8.4% ahead on decode, but the app routes this model to the REFERENCE engine, so no figure on this page is taken from it. 2026-10-04: the Ryzen AI Max+ 395 AMD rows were re-measured on the latest engines — DeepSeek-V4-Flash on antirez main + PR #992 (14.7, was 15.0) and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on the pr4 build with the selected-split env var (12.1, was 8.66-9.44). The V4.1 gap is the engine improvement, not the machine. 2026-10-04: four models added to the Ryzen row from llama.cpp llama-bench tg128 r=3 (Qwen3-4B 67.0, Qwen3-8B 38.2, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 56.1, Muse Glimmer 30B 11.5); the same instrument as the M1 Ultra's llama.cpp rows. ADDED 11 October 2026: the M1 Ultra Ternary Bonsai 2 27B row, 31.3 tok/s — the median of three whole runs, not the best of them. Method stated in the box note. It is the first row measured with repeated WHOLE RUNS rather than repetitions inside one run, and the reason is worth recording for every other row on this page: on this machine the same binary measuring the same model at the same context gave 28.33 and 31.10 tok/s in consecutive runs, each internally flat to under 1%. Repetitions inside a run measure the run; only repeating the run measures the machine. The published figure is therefore from the quieter measurement point (a 129-token prompt, spreads 1.7%, 0.1% and 0.4%) with the wider 256-token range disclosed in the note rather than averaged away. This row also differs from its neighbours in one way a reader should know: it is measured on the current engine, not on the engine in the released build.

boxes.label: M1 Ultra · 64-core GPU · 128 GB
boxes.price: from $3,999 at launch · discontinued, used market
boxes.note: Decode is short-context and measured on this machine, each model on the engine the app picks for it — and they are not the same engine. Muse Glimmer 30B is measured by a different tool and is a mean rather than a median, so it is not strictly comparable with the rows above it. GLM-5.3-Flash is quoted short-context, and its decode is a trough rather than a slope: ~14 just under 4k, where the engine's full-attention window ends, then back to ~17.8 from 8k out to 32k. Kimi-K3's out-of-core rate is carried over and has not been verified here. Ternary Bonsai 2 27B is the newest row and the one to read most carefully. Its 33.5 tok/s is the median of six interleaved whole runs at 129 tokens on 11 October 2026 (spread 32.92–34.10), with nine kernel fusions enabled, three more than reported earlier the same day; the same instrument with them off gives 29.46, so the fusions are worth +12.4% here and change no bit of the output (all 248320 logits match as bit patterns). At a 256-token prompt, 33.46 fused against 29.63 unfused clears the 32.0 tok/s goal this work was aimed at (104.6%, up from 98.3% at six fusions). The fusions are in the engine in the repository, not in build 77 or any shipped build. Separately, the model is 1.75 bits per weight, a ternary quantisation checked against a different 2-bit pack's own published continuations and agreeing on all 256 tokens of a 512-token prompt. Sizes are the real download; residency is computed from that size against this machine's memory and disk.

boxes.label: M2 Max · 64 GB
boxes.note: The same catalogue, scored for 64 GB. Every row here is measured with Low Power Mode off, but this laptop normally runs with it on, where it delivers roughly half — so these are the chip's rates, not this machine's everyday ones. DeepSeek-V4-Flash moved the most — 2.9 to 7.2 tok/s — and it does not fit in 64 GB, so that rate is experts streaming from SSD, not a resident model. Laguna-S-2.1 was re-measured at 25.8 and its published 26.4 stands. Muse Glimmer is the reminder that a tier estimate is not a promise: it reaches 0.37× the M1 Ultra here where scaling by GPU tier predicts 0.605, because how far a chip falls behind depends on how bandwidth-bound the model is. This is also the smallest M2 Max, 30 of a possible 38 GPU cores.

boxes.label: M4 mini · 16 GB
boxes.note: A 16 GB machine is offered the models that suit it, not the whole catalogue. Both rows were re-measured on this machine in August 2026, decode isolated as the difference between a 129-token and a 1-token completion so that prefill is excluded. The larger Qwen3 variants are absent because they cannot be tested here rather than because they are slow: 14B needs a download this machine has no room for, and 32B is a 20 GB file on a 16 GB machine with 12.7 GB free — it cannot be stored, let alone run.

boxes.label: DGX Spark · GB10 · 128 GB
boxes.note: The same DeepSeek-V4-Flash file on an NVIDIA GB10 Grace Blackwell desktop through the reference CUDA engine, so the model and the quantisation are comparable to the Mac rows even though the engine is not. Measured August 2026 as an A/B/B/A sequence, three repetitions per arm, GPU clock sampled throughout (2405–2535 MHz); the repetitions spanned 0.06 tok/s. The weights sit in unified memory rather than streaming, which is why an 87 GB model reports a resident rate on a 128 GB box.

boxes.label: Bosgame M5 · Ryzen AI Max+ 395 · 128 GB
boxes.note: The same DeepSeek-V4-Flash file as the DGX Spark row, on a Bosgame M5 mini-PC (AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 “Strix Halo”, 128 GB) through the reference ROCm engine. The weights sit in unified memory rather than streaming, which is why an 87 GB model reports a resident rate on a 128 GB box. The figure is the out-of-the-box power governor. Re-measured 2026-10-04 on the PR #992 build (/data/ds4-main): 14.7, consistent with the August 15.0; V4.1 re-measured 2026-10-04 at 12.1 with the pr4 engine's resident/missing MoE split (DS4_ROCM_SELECTED_SPLIT=1), up from the 8.66-9.44 August figure on the older build. The price is what was paid, not a list figure. 2026-10-04: four more Local Mind models were pulled onto this box and measured with llama.cpp's llama-bench (build 3173a56, ROCm backend on the Radeon 8060S) at tg128, r=3: Qwen3-4B 67.0, Qwen3-8B 38.2, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 56.1 (MoE), Muse Glimmer 30B 11.5. These are the same instrument and token count (128 generated) used for the M1 Ultra's llama.cpp llama-bench rows, so the two columns are directly comparable. 2026-10-04 (later): Qwen3-14B 22.1 and Laguna-XS-2.1 60.1, same llama-bench instrument. 2026-10-04 (later still): Qwen3-32B 9.7 and Qwen3.8-27B 11.0, same instrument. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next is NOT offered here: no inference engine runs it on this hardware — llama.cpp does not know its architecture, antirez ds4's ROCm path refuses it (Metal/CUDA only), and SGLang/vLLM on gfx1151 require building against TheRock nightly rather than using a packaged install. Until one of those changes, this model has no honest AMD number.

boxes.label: Atlas A2 · 8× 910B2 · 512 GB
boxes.note: Not a Local Mind machine — the app is macOS only. A Huawei Atlas A2 server: eight Ascend 910B2 cards, 64 GB HBM each, 512 GB in total, confirmed from npu-smi on the box (8 chips, 65536 MB per chip, all reporting healthy). DeepSeek-V4-Flash has not been measured here, and the attempt is worth recording. The ds4-rs-ascend controller is built and published for this hardware and installs on it. To get a decode rate, llama.cpp b10360 was built with the CANN backend on the box and the MXFP4 checkpoint (145 GB) was loaded across four 910B2 cards — then decode aborted inside ggml_cann_rope, the runtime failing to load the AI Core kernel for aclnnArange (rtsFuncGetByName ErrCode=107000). That operator passes test-backend-ops standalone on all four cards, so it is not a dead card or a missing operator package. Until it is resolved the row says 'not measured' rather than borrowing a number from another machine. The residency column reads GPU because 87 GB fits into 512 GB many times over — an arithmetic claim about capacity, not a measurement of speed. No price is shown: A2 systems sell through configuration-dependent channels with no list figure to cite, and every other price on this page names a source, so the field is left empty until there is something to point at.

boxes.label: Radeon 8060S · gfx1151 · 128 GB
boxes.note: AMD Strix Halo (gfx1151), 128 GB unified memory. ROCm 7.1.52801. MiniCPM-V 4.7 35B-A3B mixed-Q3 at 128K context. Decode 60.3–61.0 tok/s (256 tokens). 70K-token prompt recall in 141.6s. Cached follow-up in 0.757s. See minicpm-v4.7-35b-a3b-gfx1151.md for full details.
